prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, providing a theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B025 (Helpman, Melitz) and ranked B002 second. I now prefer B002 with Kiyotaki and Moore alone. There are two reasons, and neither is the number of colleagues supporting B002. First, the exchange sharpened my view of the attribution problem in B025. Fredriksson, Krusell and others stressed that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited. As I recall, but have not independently verified, the exporter-premia and selection facts that B025's 'confirmation' rests on were largely documented by that empirical strand and helped motivate the Melitz model. The firm-level evidence I weighted heavily in round 1 is therefore weaker as an out-of-sample test of the model than I credited, and it supports a prize that would be hard to confine to two names. Second, the welfare-gain channel specific to firm heterogeneity depends on functional-form assumptions, which I already flagged in round 1. B002 is a different case. The 1997 paper is a two-author origin of a mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. The mechanism has nearly three decades of theoretical, quantitative and policy use, and the 2008 crisis raised its relevance. Nobody in the exchange disputed its maturity or its credit. My main reservation, the quantitative size of the amplification, concerns magnitude and not the existence of the mechanism. I read the chair's question on B025 against B002 as one about how to weigh these criteria, and I weigh attribution clarity and conceptual originality somewhat more than I did in round 1. I keep the part at two names. A single part also respects the three-person cap without an arbitrary pairing.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. The direct identification of collateral-driven amplification, and its quantitative size, is less well established than the theory's influence suggests. As a metascience researcher I would like stronger evidence on that point. The second concern is overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. I regard this as a thematic neighbour and not a duplicate discovery, but it is a judgment the Committee must make. Third, a Kiyotaki-Moore citation leaves the financial-accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist) uncredited, and some colleagues see that strand as part of the same insight. B025 remains a serious alternative. It offers a long record of firm-level testing and a distinct mechanism from Krugman's 2008 work, but I now judge its attribution gap to be the larger obstacle. B012 has real methodological reach, but I still place it below B002 because of the seven-name credit structure and its reliance on structural assumptions, which I cannot independently verify.

responses.point: Hassler prefers Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler for B002. He argues that Gertler's later intermediary-based quantitative work, with Kiyotaki and Karadi, is separable from the 2022 recognition. He accepts the two-name version as a fallback.
responses.response: I take the separability argument seriously, and I thank the chair for stating the fallback explicitly. I would still keep the citation to Kiyotaki and Moore. The intermediary-based quantitative work is a distinct achievement from the 1997 collateral mechanism. Gertler's credit is also divided with the eight-name B043, and including him would leave Gilchrist as an obvious omission, which Hassler himself treats as outside the core. If the Committee chose the broader financial-frictions citation, I would not treat Gertler's inclusion as a reason to withhold support from B002. I would regard it as the less well-bounded version.

responses.point: Fredriksson says the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from B025 is a larger attribution problem than anything in B050. He also reports that Teorell's argument moved B002 up to his strongest alternative.
responses.response: This is the point that most changed my view. I had treated the gap as a risk to be disclosed and still ranked B025 first. After the exchange, I think it is a reason that bears on merit credit. A Helpman-Melitz citation would have to be worded carefully to avoid overstating who established the empirical regularities, and the omitted names cannot be added under the three-person cap. In B002 the credited names map onto a single founding paper. I also share his caution about reading support counts for B002 as scientific evidence. My move rests on the attribution structure, and not on how many members back it.

responses.point: Friberg keeps B025 first. He argues that Melitz changed what economists think the mechanism of trade gains is, that it is distinct from Krugman's 2008 prize, and that he could support B002 on the 1997 paper alone.
responses.response: I agree that the Melitz mechanism is distinct from Krugman's work, and I would not reject B025 on overlap grounds. Our remaining difference is about what the empirical record shows. I now think the exporter-selection facts are a weaker test of the Melitz model than I credited in round 1, since the model was built in part to rationalise them. The welfare-gain channel also depends on functional-form assumptions. Friberg's distinction between conceptual and methodological weight is fair, but it does not settle B025 against B002, because both are conceptual. I do not think his ordering is unreasonable, and I would support B025 as my first alternative if the Committee preferred it.

responses.point: Boppart argues that the 2022 prize concerned banks, runs and intermediation, while Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values on borrowers' balance sheets create a dynamic feedback loop. He says the overlap is thematic and not a duplication of the discovery.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction and it helps with the chair's question on adjacency. I would treat overlap with recent prizes as a timing and balance matter and not as scientific merit, and I would apply that principle consistently: 2008 for B025, 2022 for B002, and 2024 for B050 and B021. Under that principle the 2022 overlap does not lower B002's merit, though the Committee may weigh it for balance. I also share his reservation that empirical identification of the amplification magnitude is weaker than the theory. On the chair's evidence request, I would accept well-identified micro or regional studies in which shocks to collateral values, such as property or land prices, move firm borrowing and investment. I recall such work exists but have not verified it. I would not change a ranking on that basis within this round.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B012 first and says a Committee that places conceptual discovery above measurement would reasonably favour B002 or B025. She also treats the three-name limit as a constraint on the citation and not as evidence against the discovery.
responses.response: I agree that the three-name limit is not a flaw in the candidate itself, and that BLP is a measurement framework with economic content and not only a statistical device. For that reason I called my earlier B012 ranking a judgment about attribution and not about quality. My difficulty is that the credit structure matters for this decision. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are credited on the ballot, and she herself notes that if Bresnahan were judged equal in kind, no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible. B002 does not have that problem. I accept that members who weigh methods more heavily than I do could reasonably rank B012 higher.

uncertainties: How large collateral-driven amplification is quantitatively, and whether the available identification would satisfy a committee that weights empirical confirmation heavily. I cannot verify the empirical literature beyond my recollection.

Whether the Committee reads the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as covering the collateral-constraint mechanism. I treat the overlap as thematic, but that is a judgment and not a settled fact.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist makes a Kiyotaki-Moore citation look incomplete relative to the financial-accelerator literature.

My recollection that the exporter-premia facts were documented by Bernard, Jensen and others, and helped motivate the Melitz model, is not independently verified. It drives my move away from B025, so my ordering of B025 against B002 is sensitive to it.

Whether B025 or B001 is the better fallback if B002 fails. B001 depends on whether game theory faces a higher threshold, and on whether the Rubinstein-Wolinsky market-bargaining work should share credit with the 1982 result.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Rubinstein, Wolinsky and Binmore do not appear among my listed co-authors or networks (Johannesson, Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak, Ellingsen, Almenberg, Brodeur). My research in behavioural economics and metascience is not adjacent to macro-finance or international trade. I disclose that my main co-author, Magnus Johannesson, is a former committee member, but he is not a candidate. I note that my change from B025 to B002 follows the round-1 exchange. I do not treat that as a conflict, and I do not adjudicate any colleague's disclosures.
